question: For a Class A or B CDL, a tank endorsement is required to haul a liquid or liquid gas in a tank meeting which capacity description?
choice_a: An aggregate rated capacity of exactly 500 gallons
choice_b: Any tank permanently welded to the frame, regardless of size
choice_c: Any single tank over 55 gallons, regardless of aggregate capacity
choice_d: An individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more
explanation: A tank endorsement is required when hauling liquid or liquid gas in a tank or tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more, permanently or temporarily attached to the vehicle or chassis.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 87

question: On all tank vehicles, what is the single most important item to check during inspection?
choice_c: Leaks, checked under and around the vehicle
explanation: The manual states that on all tank vehicles, the most important item to check for is leaks, checking under and around the vehicle for any signs of leaking.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 88

question: What happens if you carry liquids or gases in a leaking tank?
choice_a: You must simply note it on the trip report and continue
choice_b: Nothing, as long as the leak is minor and away from the driver
choice_c: It is a crime; you will be cited, prevented from driving further, and may be liable for spill clean-up
choice_d: It only becomes a violation if the leak exceeds one gallon per hour
explanation: Don't carry liquids or gases in a leaking tank -- to do so is a crime, you will be cited and prevented from driving further, and you may also be liable for the clean-up of any spill.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 88

question: When inspecting the intake, discharge, and cutoff valves on a tank vehicle, what must you confirm?
choice_a: That they are labeled in a language you can read
choice_b: That they were replaced within the last year
choice_c: That the valves are in the correct position before loading, unloading, or moving the vehicle
choice_d: That they are painted to match the tank color
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to check the intake, discharge, and cutoff valves, making sure the valves are in the correct position before loading, unloading, or moving the vehicle.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 88

question: During inspection, what should you check about manhole covers and vents?
choice_a: That the covers match the color of the tank shell
choice_b: That the covers have gaskets and close correctly, and that vents are kept clear so they work correctly
choice_c: That the covers are bolted shut permanently and never opened
choice_d: That the vents are taped over to prevent any airflow
explanation: The manual directs drivers to check manhole covers and vents, making sure the covers have gaskets and close correctly, and to keep the vents clear so they work correctly.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 88

question: If your tank vehicle has a vapor recovery kit, grounding and bonding cables, an emergency shut-off system, and a built-in fire extinguisher, what must you verify before driving?
choice_a: That they are listed on the bill of lading
choice_b: That they are all present, working correctly, and functional
choice_c: Only that the fire extinguisher exists; the rest are optional
choice_d: That they have been removed for the current trip
explanation: If your vehicle has vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, or a built-in fire extinguisher, make sure they work.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 88

topic: Never Drive With Open Valves or Covers
question: According to the manual, what should you never do with a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Park it on a level surface
choice_b: Drive it with open valves or manhole covers
choice_c: Drive it below the posted speed limit
choice_d: Drive it with less than a full load
explanation: The manual explicitly states you should never drive a tank vehicle with open valves or manhole covers.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 88

question: Why are liquid tankers especially prone to rolling over?
choice_a: Their tires are narrower than standard truck tires
choice_b: They lack a fifth wheel locking mechanism
choice_c: They are always dispatched with an unbalanced fuel load
choice_d: Their high center of gravity carries much of the load's weight high off the road, making them top-heavy
explanation: High center of gravity means much of the load's weight is carried high up off the road, making the vehicle top-heavy and easy to roll over; tests have shown tankers can turn over at the speed limits posted for curves.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 88

question: Since tests show tankers can roll over even at the speed limit posted for a curve, how should a tank vehicle driver approach highway curves and on-ramp/off-ramp curves?
choice_a: Ignore posted curve speeds since they only apply to passenger vehicles
choice_b: Take them well below the posted speeds
choice_c: Take them exactly at the posted speed to stay with traffic flow
choice_d: Take them slightly above the posted speed if the tank is empty
explanation: Because tankers can turn over at the speed limits posted for curves, drivers must take highway curves and on-ramp/off-ramp curves well below the posted speeds.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 88

question: What is "liquid surge" as it applies to tank vehicles?
choice_a: The rate at which liquid expands when warmed
choice_b: The buildup of static electricity while unloading a tank
choice_c: A pressure spike caused by a closed cutoff valve
choice_d: Movement of liquid in a partially filled tank, such as surging back and forth when coming to a stop
explanation: Liquid surge results from movement of the liquid in partially filled tanks; for example, when coming to a stop, the liquid will surge back and forth, and when the wave hits the end of the tank it tends to push the truck in the direction the wave is moving.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 88

question: What extra danger does liquid surge create on a slippery surface such as ice?
choice_a: The bulkheads will crack from the cold
choice_b: The trailer brakes will lock permanently
choice_c: The surging wave can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection
choice_d: The tank will automatically vent to relieve pressure
explanation: If the truck is on a slippery surface such as ice, the surge wave can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection, which is why the driver of a liquid tanker must be very familiar with the vehicle's handling.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 88

question: Some liquid tanks are divided into smaller tanks by bulkheads. What must a driver pay attention to when loading and unloading these smaller compartments?
choice_b: The compartment's paint color coding only
choice_a: Weight distribution, so as not to put too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle
choice_c: The brand of liquid stored in the adjacent compartment
choice_d: The order in which each compartment was manufactured
explanation: When loading and unloading the smaller tanks created by bulkheads, the driver must pay attention to weight distribution and avoid putting too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 89

question: How do baffled liquid tanks help control surge, and what limitation do they have?
choice_a: They only control side-to-side surge, not forward-and-backward surge
choice_b: They use electronic sensors to stop liquid movement entirely
choice_c: Bulkheads with holes let liquid flow through to control forward-and-backward surge, but side-to-side surge can still occur and cause a rollover
choice_d: They eliminate all forms of surge in every direction
explanation: Baffled liquid tanks have bulkheads in them with holes that let the liquid flow through, which helps control forward and backward liquid surge; however, side-to-side surge can still occur and this can cause a rollover.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 89

question: Un-baffled ("smooth bore") tanks, commonly used for food products like milk, have nothing inside to slow the liquid's flow. What must a driver do as a result?
choice_a: Be extremely cautious, slow and careful, especially when starting and stopping, because forward-and-back surge is very strong
choice_b: Drive faster than usual to keep the liquid from settling
choice_c: Add baffles before every trip to compensate
choice_d: Fill the tank completely to eliminate any surge
explanation: Un-baffled tankers have nothing inside to slow the flow of liquid, so forward-and-back surge is very strong; sanitation regulations forbid baffles in tanks like milk tankers because of cleaning difficulty, so the driver must be extremely cautious, especially when starting and stopping.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 89

question: What is "outage" when loading a cargo tank?
choice_a: The time a tank sits empty between loads
choice_b: Room deliberately left unfilled so liquid can expand as it warms, since you must never load a cargo tank totally full
choice_c: A mechanical failure of the outlet valve
choice_d: A recorded shortage of delivered product at the destination
explanation: You must never load a cargo tank totally full because liquids expand as they warm and you must leave room for the expanding liquid; this is called outage, and different liquids require different amounts of outage.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 89

question: What braking approach helps a driver control liquid surge when bringing a tank vehicle to a stop?
choice_a: Keep a steady pressure on the brakes, not releasing too soon, and brake far in advance while increasing following distance
choice_b: Release the brakes early so the surging liquid can settle before the vehicle fully stops
choice_c: Pump the brakes rapidly and repeatedly throughout the stop
choice_d: Steer sharply while braking to counteract the surge
explanation: To control surge, keep a steady pressure on the brakes and do not release too soon when coming to a stop; also brake far in advance of a stop and increase your following distance. Steering quickly while braking can cause the vehicle to roll over.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 89

question: What does the manual say about stopping distance for tank vehicles?
choice_a: Stopping distance is identical for tank vehicles regardless of road conditions
choice_b: Full tank vehicles always require more distance to stop than empty ones
choice_c: Wet roads double the normal stopping distance, and empty tank vehicles may take longer to stop than full ones
choice_d: Wet roads have no measurable effect on a tank vehicle's stopping distance
explanation: The manual warns drivers to keep in mind how much space is needed to stop; wet roads double the normal stopping distance, and empty tank vehicles may actually take longer to stop than full ones.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 89

question: On a tank trailer, what can happen if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid from over steering, over accelerating, or over braking?
choice_a: The bulkheads shift to rebalance the load
choice_b: The parking brake engages automatically to stop the skid
choice_d: The tank will automatically release pressure to correct the skid
explanation: Don't over steer, over accelerate, or over brake, as this can cause a skid; on tank trailers, if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid, the vehicle may jackknife, and the driver must take action to restore traction.
source_note: Colorado CDL Manual (2023 CDL Testing System, DR 2251, June 2023), Colorado Department of Revenue - Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 89
